name: Surrender — the cognitive surrender test for your own pull requests
one_liner: Paste any public GitHub PR URL (yours or someone else's) and Surrender quizzes you on it the way a sharp reviewer would — five questions straight from the diff, graded in 20 seconds — then gives you a shareable "Surrender Score" card and a weekly streak of the PRs you actually understood.
problem: Developers now merge code an agent wrote in minutes. Addy Osmani's Nov 3 piece named the slide: cognitive offloading → deferral → "cognitive surrender", where you approve polished output you don't understand. Everyone recognises the feeling and nobody measures it. Today the workarounds are manual prompts ("explain this code back to me") copy-pasted from Reddit threads, or install-first tools (Sphinx git hook, PRcheck GitHub App, vibecheck.dev self-hosted) that require setup and team buy-in before you learn anything about yourself. There is no zero-install, paste-a-link way to find out in 30 seconds whether you could defend the diff you just merged.
target_customer: Individual developers shipping agent-written code daily — the Cursor/Claude Code/Codex crowd on X, r/ExperiencedDevs, r/ChatGPTCoding and HN. Also tech leads who will run it on their team's merged PRs and post the result. Free; the user brings their own Gemini API key (free tier exists) so there is no cost to the builder.
why_now: Three things landed in the last few weeks: (1) Addy Osmani's "cognitive surrender" article on Nov 3 2026 put a name on the problem and did 21k likes in the builder's own bookmarks (https://x.com/addyosmani/status/2117512471930167377); (2) GitHub's REST API serves a PR diff client-side with CORS and no auth at 60 req/hr/IP, so the whole thing is a static page (https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/pulls); (3) Gemini 3 Flash ($0.50/$3 per M tokens, free tier, browser-callable with the user's own key) makes five good diff-grounded questions cost a fraction of a cent (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing). The category exists but is all install-first: Sphinx is a git hook at ~461 stars, PRcheck is an early GitHub App, LiveReview ~156 stars. Nobody has shipped the zero-install, shareable version.
comparables: Sphinx (https://github.com/parthh01/sphinx) — git pre-push hook that quizzes you; ~461 stars, requires install and gates local pushes, no share card. PRcheck (https://github.com/samsasmm/prcheck, https://www.producthunt.com/p/prcheck/prcheck) — pre-merge "explain-back" GitHub check, early stage, team workflow, needs App install. vibecheck.dev (https://github.com/bhurghundii/vibecheck.dev) — self-hosted, needs an Anthropic key and setup. LiveReview (https://github.com/HexmosTech/LiveReview) — quiz mode inside a code-review product, ~156 stars. Save Point (https://github.com/thierrypdamiba/save-point) — alpha agent skill, post-merge quiz, local state. Research (Perplexity, two calls) found no free no-install web app where you paste a PR URL and get graded, and no shareable score card or streak anywhere in the category. Surrender's difference: no install, works on any public PR including other people's, output is a card built to be posted, and a weekly streak gives a reason to come back.
market_note: Not a market play — a free open-source tool. Estimate: the audience is anyone merging agent code, which is now most working developers; the realistic ceiling is a viral weekend (tens of thousands of runs) plus a long tail of team leads running it on their repos. Zero marginal cost because users bring their own API key. If it grew, the paid version is the team dashboard (which PRcheck is already chasing), not this.
risks: 1) Grading is the whole product and an LLM grader can be wrong or pedantic — one unfair "you failed" and the user closes the tab. Mitigation: show the exact diff lines each answer was graded against, and let the user contest ("I think I was right") which flips the grade and is itself shareable. 2) It can read as an insult; people don't post failures. Mitigation: frame the card as a confidence score with a funny tier name, and make "I scored 2/5 on my own PR" the joke people want to tell on themselves — self-deprecation posts well on dev X. 3) Typing five free-text answers is a lot of friction versus one click; if answers are long people bail. Mitigation: short-answer boxes with a "good enough" grader, and a 90-second visible target.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) People will type real answers instead of bouncing — the whole value needs ~90 seconds of effort, far more than a one-click toy. 2) The grader feels fair on a first try with a real diff; if it nitpicks, trust collapses immediately. 3) Developers will post a low score about their own code rather than quietly closing the tab.
first_customers: The replies under Addy Osmani's cognitive-surrender article (21k likes, 618 replies) — run it on a famous public PR and post the card there. Then r/ExperiencedDevs ("how do you evaluate engineers when everyone's using AI coding tools"), r/ChatGPTCoding, the Cursor and Claude Code Discords, and HN Show HN where Sphinx already found 461 stars of interested people.
validation_test: Ship the static page, then post one thing: run Surrender on a PR from your own public repo, screenshot the card with your real (bad) score, and reply to the Osmani thread plus Show HN. Pass = 300+ completed quizzes in week one and at least 20 people posting their own card unprompted. Fail = people open it, read the questions and never answer one; the drop-off between "questions shown" and "first answer submitted" is the single metric to watch.
build_plan: Stack: one static page (TypeScript + Vite, deploy to Vercel/Pages), no backend. Data: GitHub REST `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/pulls/{n}` with `Accept: application/vnd.github.diff` — CORS-enabled, unauthenticated, 60 req/hr/IP, optional user PAT field to raise it. Model: Gemini 3 Flash via `x-goog-api-key` from the browser with the user's own key (free tier available); fall back to a hard-coded demo PR if no key. Steps: (1) PR URL in → fetch diff, truncate to the 5 largest hunks under ~40k chars; (2) one model call returns 5 questions, each tagged with the file+line range it comes from and a short rubric; (3) five short-answer boxes, one call grades all five against the rubric and the diff, returns pass/partial/fail plus the exact lines you missed; (4) render a Surrender Score card to canvas → PNG download + prefilled X intent link; (5) localStorage streak: PRs quizzed this week, running average, "you last understood your code 4 days ago". Cut for v1: GitHub login, private repos, teams, leaderboards, any backend, storing anything server-side.
launch_post:
Addy Osmani called it cognitive surrender: approving code you don't actually understand.

So I built the test. Paste any public GitHub PR, answer 5 questions a sharp reviewer would ask, get graded against the real diff.

I scored 2/5 on my own PR. Free, no login, open source.
reasoning:
Beat the field because it is the only candidate where a bookmark supplied both the problem and the audience in the same week. Osmani's "cognitive surrender" post (21k likes, 618 replies) is a named feeling with no measuring stick, and the builder's taste file wants one input box → one striking output → a free open-source static page; a PR URL in and a graded score card out is exactly that shape. The category check was the deciding evidence: Sphinx (461 stars), PRcheck and vibecheck all prove people want this, and all three require an install or a self-host before you learn anything, which is why none of them spread. A zero-install page that works on any public PR — including a famous repo's PR, so you can quiz yourself on someone else's code — is the version that gets posted.

Builds on no past idea's workflow. The nearest neighbours in the library are Ghostwritten (measures what share of a repo an agent wrote, with a quiz as a side feature) and Blindspot (maps untouched agent-written files). Both are repo-level forensics: you paste a repo, you get a map of the past. Surrender is a single-PR, before-you-merge act you perform on yourself, graded live, with a streak — different unit of analysis, different moment, different output. It deliberately does not reuse Ghostwritten's attribution idea at all; nothing here guesses who wrote the code.

No overlap with tonight's venture (Declined, insurance E&O decision records for P&C agencies): different audience, different problem, different workflow. No investor signal was used; a16z's "cognitive" and agent-reliability themes are adjacent but bending this to them would have made it worse.

could_grow is true but unexciting: the obvious business is a team dashboard of comprehension scores, which PRcheck is already building and which managers would weaponise. The honest read is that this is a great weekend project and a mediocre company.

Honest scoring note: usefulness stayed at 7 because the streak is a designed reason to return, not a verified one — no evidence exists that developers will quiz themselves weekly. 8.0 overall reflects strong wow/shareability/buildability/freshness against a soft retention case.

Runner-up (Venture, 7.6): Tonight's bookmarks are mostly developer-tool noise, but one of them is a genuine market event: Claude Meetings putting an AI participant inside Google Meet for every Team/Enterprise customer. The interesting consequence is not better notes — it is that regulated professionals are now generating discoverable transcripts of advice conversations. Two E&O carriers published guidance about exactly this in 2026 (Utica's "Before You Record"; Berkley's declination guidance), which is the kind of third-party pressure that creates a budget line. Declined wins over the other finalists because the buyer is named and already spends on the problem in three visible ways — E&O premium, outsourced back-office (ReSource Pro explicitly lists proposal and comparison work), and InsurGrid's $99/month manual declination e-sign product — and because the artefact is legible: a typed coverage ledger plus a signed acknowledgment is something a principal can picture in a thirty-second demo. It builds on no past idea's buyer: Shortfall (2026-11-03) also serves independent P&C agencies, but that is a commissions-reconciliation product for the owner's money, with a completely different workflow and data source; Declined is a client-conversation-to-record product for the producer/account manager, and none of the past ideas touch it. Bouncer was the closest conceptual neighbour and I dropped the bot-governance angle entirely to avoid repeating it — Declined deliberately does not care which bot joined; it cares what was decided. Honest weak spots, reflected in the 7s: Zocks has the capital, the capture layer and an insurance go-to-market, and is one schema away from this, so the gap is "room, confirmed by what incumbents don't do" rather than "nobody is near"; and the wedge is 7 not 8 because a genuinely sellable version needs the review gate plus the e-sign chain, which is more than a weekend — though the paste-into-Epic version is shippable in roughly a month. This is an expressed pain: agencies already buy forms, courses and outsourcing to manage it, and carriers write bulletins about it.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Declined — coverage-decision record from renewal conversations for commercial P&C agencies. PICK. Named buyer, carrier guidance published in 2026, a manual-form incumbent (InsurGrid) proving willingness to pay, and nothing found that goes conversation → typed decision ledger → signed acknowledgment → AMS.
2. Meeting-artefact governance for regulated firms (who recorded, which bot, consent) — DROPPED as a repeat: Bouncer (2026-11-15) serves the RIA CCO with essentially this workflow.
3. Mobile approval layer for remote coding agents (from @KlausCodes and DigitalOcean Cuttlefish) — dropped at screen. HumanLayer (YC F24), Auth0 for AI Agents, n8n and now DigitalOcean itself all sell the approve/deny loop; buyer is the crowded dev-tools market the builder is already over-indexed on, and past ideas (Doublecheck, Ledger, Driftwatch) sit nearby.
4. City-clerk minutes-to-motions record (AI for City Hall RFS + Claude Meetings) — finalist, lost. Real pain, but ClerkMinutes publishes $1,188-$2,988/yr plans, CivicPlus and eScribe both ship AI minutes, and the procurement cycle is brutal for a solo evening-and-weekend founder. Gap would have scored 5.
5. Architect/engineer design-decision log from client meetings (change-order defence) — finalist, lost. Same artefact shape as Declined and genuinely underserved, but the buyer is more fragmented, there is no third-party body (like an E&O carrier) telling them to do it, and past idea Backcheck already works the AEC permit buyer.
6. "Plaid for government benefits" document-verification helper for nonprofit benefit navigators (YC RFS) — dropped at screen. Buyer is grant-funded with no software budget line, sales cycle measured in quarters, and the data-access side is the actual hard part.
7. Agent fleet console for agents running on remote laptops/sandboxes (from @KlausCodes + Apple container clustering) — dropped at screen: infrastructure play, platform vendors are shipping it, no clear SMB buyer.
8. Post-incident security-posture attestation for small software vendors answering customer questionnaires after the Nov 2026 incidents (from Jack Cable's guide) — dropped at screen. Vanta/Drata adjacency, and past ideas Blastdoor/SkillProof/Nearmiss already mine this seam.
9. "Critical thinking gate" / review-before-merge record for agent-written work (from Addy Osmani) — dropped at screen: too close to Blindspot and Ghostwritten, and no budget holder.
10. Friction-removal micro-investing for an underserved region (from @misbahspeaks / SIPSea) — dropped at generate: consumer fintech, heavy regulation, wrong fit for this builder's time and skills.
11. Vendor-change watcher for commercial insurance (carrier form/endorsement changes) — dropped at generate: overlaps Driftwatch's pattern and FurtherAI/policy-checking vendors already occupy it.

PROJECT
1. Surrender — paste a GitHub PR URL, get quizzed by a reviewer-grade AI on the real diff, shareable score card + weekly streak. PICK. Only candidate where the problem was named in a bookmark this month, the prior art is all install-first, and every dependency is free and browser-side.
2. Blast Radius Card — paste your MCP config / extension list, see what a compromised laptop reaches, as a poster. FINALIST, lost. Deep research found pisan-labs/agent-blast-radius already does pasted-config browser scoring, plus blastmap, Kloudle's Agent Blast Radius, mcpindex.ai and secret-blast-radius. Crowded in the last two months, and too close to the library's Blastdoor and Strangers.
3. Untangle Score — paste a repo, get a copy-paste/leaky-abstraction map as a shareable image. FINALIST, lost. GitDiagram, CodeFlow, jscpd and CodeScene cover the ground; static analysis of an arbitrary repo in the browser is a real weekend risk; and the output is a chart nobody posts about themselves.
4. Cooldown Check — show which deps a 7-day cooldown would have blocked. Dropped at screen: Dependabot ships a 7-day cooldown natively now, and the library already has Freshline, Nearmiss and Strangers on exactly this lockfile-paste workflow.
5. Laundry Agent — location-based nagging reminders from one sentence, per @trq212. Dropped at screen: verified that iOS Safari cannot do background geofencing (W3C Geolocation CRD, Oct 2026), so a static page physically cannot deliver the one thing that matters.
6. Agent Switchboard — one web UI to see and approve all agents running on remote machines (@KlausCodes' question, DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish). Dropped at screen: needs a daemon on every machine plus a relay — weeks, not a weekend, and nothing to screenshot.
7. Mac Cluster in a Box — a one-click local k8s playground on Apple container 1.7.1 (released Nov 6 2026). Dropped at screen: genuinely fresh, but it's a CLI wrapper for Apple-silicon owners only, with no shareable output and no reason to return.
8. Meeting Artifact — paste a transcript, get a whiteboard diagram (riffing on Claude Meetings). Dropped at screen: Claude, Copilot and a dozen notetakers own this, and the builder would be cloning a product named in the bookmark.
9. Security Debt Scorecard — turn Jack Cable's guide into a self-audit with a grade. Dropped at screen: checkbox quizzes don't spread, the output is self-reported, and it overlaps the library's security-hygiene cluster.
10. Review Time Receipt — how many seconds you spent on each PR you approved. Dropped at screen: GitHub exposes no reliable per-reviewer dwell time, so the central number would be fabricated.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3 of 3): summarised Claude Meetings (confirmed Google Meet, Team/Enterprise, beta, transcript export to Otter/Fireflies/Granola planned — this is what makes recorded advice conversations ubiquitous), DigitalOcean Cuttlefish (confirmed it is a control/approval surface tied to Managed Agents, and that mobile agent approval is not yet proven as a standalone category — killed candidate 3), and Jack Cable's Nov 2026 security guide (confirmed the incident cluster behind candidate 8; dropped as too close to past ideas). A fourth summary on Addy Osmani's article was spent from the screening pot and shaped candidate 9.
Screening pot (6 of 6): AI-notetaker consent/compliance landscape (found Kolmogorov Law's 2026 survey claim that notetakers joined 1 in 3 workers' meetings and that only a third were always asked — supports the timing but pointed at past idea Bouncer, so I pivoted away from consent); human-in-the-loop approval market (HumanLayer, Auth0, n8n — killed candidate 3); AEC design-decision logs (real but unfocused buyer, candidate 5 kept as finalist then dropped); insurance AI tooling landscape (surfaced Zocks/Jump as the dominant adjacency); dev-laptop security posture (thin, killed candidate 8); benefits eligibility verification (only policy manuals, no buyer evidence, killed candidate 6).
Deep-research pot (12 of 12): city-clerk minutes vendors and pricing (ClerkMinutes $1,188-$2,988/yr, CivicPlus AI minutes as paid add-on, eScribe, Granicus ~$10.2k/yr contract example — closed the gap on candidate 4 and eliminated it); Zocks/Jump/Sixfold/Comulate coverage of broker meetings and AMS write-back (found Zocks closest but AMS write-back unverified, Sixfold and Comulate different buyers); E&O documentation standards and failure-to-procure claim context; Zocks and Jump pricing plus E&O-suitability check; E&O claim severity, agency counts and premiums ($50k+ defence benchmark, 37,000 agencies, $3-8k agency E&O premium estimate); declination-tracking vendor search (first pass found none); E&O carrier credits (Utica, Swiss Re, Berkley); Swiss Re checklist and Big "I" E&O Guardian credit detail; whether any tool generates signed declinations from conversations (no); Zocks' own E&O-liability post on transcripts; the post-renewal proposal/acknowledgment workflow and outsourcing prices (ReSource Pro, Patra, ~$1,800-$7,000/FTE/mo directional); and the Indio/Broker Buddha/Zywave proposal-signature sweep, which finally surfaced InsurGrid's declination e-sign — the single most important find, because it proves agencies pay for the artefact manually.
Sharpening pot (5 of 5): InsurGrid pricing and whether its declination flow is manual (confirmed manual, $79-99/mo, no conversation detection); policy-checking and documentation time plus evidence of E&O-transcript anxiety (found Utica's explicit discovery warning; found only vendor estimates — ~8 hrs for a complex policy check, 15-25 min per client call — which is why pain is 8 not 9); Utica's "Before You Record" guidance in full; Big "I"/IIAT adoption of signed coverage checklists (found the honest counter-evidence that universal signed checklists are unrealistic and that a signature is not a shield — this is why wedge stayed at 7 and why the build plan defaults to proof-of-sending with signature as an upgrade); and the two IA Magazine pieces on rising E&O claims and how exposure is built into workflow.
Investor signals weighed: YC W27 Vertical Foundation Models (typed decision instead of generated text — directly shapes the extraction design), YC W27 AI for City Hall (drove candidate 4, which research then killed), YC W27 The $15-an-Hour Expert and Plaid for Government Benefits (candidate 6, no budget found), a16z Big Ideas 2026 "AI will finally upgrade banking and insurance infrastructure" and "systems of record lose ground" (both support the pick's thesis that the record, not the workflow UI, is the contested asset). No signal was adopted as the idea itself.
Sharpening (7 to 7.6): Round 1 — weak criterion: gap (6 before). Pre-sharpen idea was "AI meeting record for insurance agents", which collides head-on with Zocks ($45M Series B, $67-184/user/mo, now marketing a P&C workflow) and Jump ($80M Series B). Change: moved the wedge off "notes" entirely and onto the one artefact none of them produce — a typed, coverage-by-coverage offered/recommended/accepted/declined ledger plus the client-signed declination acknowledgment. Research found: Zocks' own blog warns that transcripts bury declinations and can contradict the official file; InsurGrid sells a manual declination/LPR e-sign workflow at $79-99/mo and is the only product found that touches the artefact, but a human must prepare and send it, and it does nothing with conversations; Broker Buddha and Applied's Collaboration Portal e-sign applications and proposals, not declinations. Gap 6 → 7 (not higher: Zocks is adjacent and well-funded). Pain 7 → 8 on Berkley's March 2026 declination guidance and IA Magazine's Nov 2026 piece confirming files turn on exactly this record.
Round 2 — weak criterion: market_pull (7 before). Change: moved the buyer from the producer who feels the pain to the agency principal/E&O-compliance owner who signs the E&O cheque, and added the E&O carrier and Big "I" state association as a distribution channel rather than just a talking point. Research found: Swiss Re/Westport's comparison checklist documents a 10% risk-management-course credit, up to 20% loss-free credit and a five-year 10% credit for completing a risk-management audit, and some program guidance lists coverage checklists with insured sign-offs on declined coverages as a route to a credit subject to underwriter review; Utica advertises a loss-control credit but ties it to exposure analysis and training, not tools. So the credit is real but NOT automatic for buying software — I did not lift timing on this, and market_pull went 7 → 8 (a named role with a budget line and comparable per-seat prices found: Zocks, Jump, InsurGrid, Epic seat estimates) rather than 9, because I found no agency publicly paying for this exact record. Score 7.0 → 7.6.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised Apple container 1.7.1's cluster.md (confirmed k8s-on-Mac, released Nov 6 2026 — killed candidate 7 as a CLI with no shareable output); Jack Cable's security guide (gave the real content behind the ScottWu46/jackhcable bookmark — seeded candidates 2, 4 and 9 and specifically the "a compromised laptop must not reach production" and 7-day-cooldown lines); Addy Osmani's untitled article link, which turned out to be the "cognitive surrender" essay — this single call produced the winning candidate, since the bookmark's own text was just a bare URL.

Screening pot (5/5): one search each on extension/permission audit tools, location-reminder side projects, meeting-transcript-to-diagram tools, GitHub Archive wrapped-style tools, and "blast radius" tools. The blast-radius search surfaced the Endor Labs Binance write-up and confirmed the theme was hot; the GH Archive search came back empty of competition but also of inspiration.

Deep-research pot (8/8): (a) prior art on code-comprehension quizzes → found Sphinx, PRcheck, Save Point, vibecheck.dev, establishing the category is real but install-first; (b) popularity check → Sphinx ~461 stars, LiveReview ~156, vibecheck self-hosted with an Anthropic key — niche, nobody owns it; (c) GitHub REST diff access from the browser → CORS allowed, unauthenticated, 60 req/hr/IP, 300-file/1MB diff caps, which set the truncation rule in the build plan; (d) blast-radius prior art → five competing tools incl. a browser pasted-config one, killing finalist 2; (e) repo-duplication visualisers → GitDiagram/jscpd/CodeScene, killing finalist 3; (f) stale-file maps and repo posters → no match but no spark either; (g) iOS background geolocation → killed the laundry candidate outright; (h) weekly GitHub leaderboards → no PR-size/reviewability leaderboard exists, which is why the streak was made personal rather than public.

Sharpening pot (4/4): two calls on whether anything tracks comprehension over time or ships a share card/streak (nothing does — Copilot and Claude dashboards only count AI-attributed PRs); one call on PR "reviewability"/risk scoring prior art (all measure size, complexity or risk, none ask the author questions); one call verifying Gemini 3 Flash pricing ($0.50/$3 per M, free tier) and that a browser app can call it with a user-supplied key. The last call is what let buildability sit at 9 rather than 7 — no backend, no cost to the builder.
Sharpening (7.4 to 8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (6, a one-time toy: quiz yourself once, laugh, leave). Change: added the weekly streak strip — localStorage history of every PR you've been quizzed on, a running average, and the "last time you cleanly explained your own code was N days ago" line, so the tool becomes a personal habit meter rather than a single test. Research (Perplexity: "how many merged PRs could I not explain" dashboards; Perplexity: Sphinx/PRcheck/vibecheck feature check) found GitHub's Copilot dashboard and Claude's analytics count AI-attributed PRs but nothing measures or tracks comprehension over time, and none of Sphinx, PRcheck, vibecheck or LiveReview has a streak or shareable card. Usefulness 6 → 7 (capped: I could not verify people actually return weekly, only that nothing competes). Shareability 7 → 8 on the same evidence, since no competitor ships a postable artifact.
Round 2 — weak criterion: wow (7, "a quiz" sounds dull). Change: the questions are grounded in specific diff lines and the result shows the exact lines you missed, plus an "I think I was right" contest button that turns the grader from judge into argument — the surprising moment is a stranger's tool asking a question about your code that is sharper than your actual reviewer got. Research (Perplexity: PR "reviewability"/comprehension scoring prior art) confirmed existing PR scorers measure complexity, size or risk — AI Code Reviewer's 0-100 complexity score, MicroReview, pr-risk-score — and none produce reviewer-style comprehension questions with a per-PR author-facing grade; also confirmed GitHub serves PR diffs client-side with CORS so the questions can be built from the real diff in a static page. Wow 7 → 8. Buildability held at 9 (diff fetch, Gemini pricing and browser CORS all verified; one static page, user's own key).
prototype_summary: Surrender is a clickable prototype that quizzes you on a pasted GitHub PR with five diff-grounded questions, grades your answers locally, and produces a shareable score card plus a streak strip.
